title: Changing Someone’s Mind

fn.en: Give opinions and try to change somebody’s opinion; write a summary.

gr: conceding a point and then arguing against it

can.en: I can concede what is true in somebody’s argument and still change their mind.

acts.title: The argument we have every year
text: Every year somebody in this office argues that a good ___ matters more than enjoying the work.
The other side says that enjoyment has to be the ___, because you spend so much of your life there.
The ___ answer is that you need enough of the first and as much as possible of the second.
What nobody says out loud is that being ___ with a job you dislike is much easier at twenty-five than at fifty.
The best manager I ever had was ___ without ever pretending the work was interesting.
That is the part I would ___ to the other side, and the only part.

items.q: Shall I ___ you, or can you manage on your own?
Google is not a ___ company.
Another perk for Google employees is free ___ checks.
Twenty engineers have been ___ for the James Dyson Award.
The idea for the Airdrop came from the Namib ___.
If you ___ into colleagues all the time, you will share more ideas.
Suncayr ___ you from sunburn.
Too little light and too much light can both ___ productivity.

tts: I have to say that, for me, the most important quality of a teacher is being patient. Teachers need to understand that it is not necessarily that easy to learn something. And being kind is important too.

Well, you have got a point, but if they are actually going to teach you something, they need to be more than kind and patient. They need to have good ideas — to be creative, to come up with something that will make the lesson interesting and fun.
Yes, but on the other hand, sometimes teachers create really fun lessons and you do not learn anything. I am all for having fun, but I do want to get more than that out of the class, don’t you?
Oh yes, obviously that is important.
But I still want them to be encouraging and supportive.
No, but look — it is possible for a teacher to be too nice sometimes, isn’t it?

items.q: What are the two speakers disagreeing about?
o: Which quality matters most in a teacher

items.q: What does the second speaker argue?
o: Kindness and patience are not enough on their own

items.q: What does “No, but look…” signal?
o: A firm disagreement, softened by the opening

tts: I do really enjoy my job, but I also earn quite a good salary, so I guess I am lucky. But if I had to choose, I would choose to enjoy my job over the money. You spend so much of your life at work that you have to enjoy it, or life is just miserable.
Well, you have got a point, but if you do not have enough money you can be pretty miserable too, can’t you?
As I see it, you do not need loads of money, but you do need enough, so that has to be the priority. If you do not enjoy your job, you can always do things you enjoy in your free time.
Yes, but don’t you think you should change jobs if you hate what you are doing?

items.s: The first speaker earns a reasonable salary and enjoys the work.
The second speaker argues that money is irrelevant.
The third speaker says enough money has to be the priority.
The third speaker suggests enjoying life outside work instead.
Everybody in the conversation agrees by the end.

acts.title: La Belle Époque
tts: From 1878 to 1914, Western Europe enjoyed an era of peace and prosperity. People had more time and more money, so they could enjoy themselves and express themselves more than ever before. It was a time of great optimism and creativity, and at its centre was Paris.

The Eiffel Tower is now a symbol of France, but it originally served as a temporary entrance to the 1889 World Fair. The French government had it built to celebrate the hundredth anniversary of the French revolution, and at three hundred and twenty-four metres it was the tallest structure in the world for over forty years.

This mixture of art and science was a popular theme. All over the city, scientists, engineers, architects and artists were combining knowledge to create buildings and objects that were not only functional but beautiful too.

This reached its highpoint at the city’s next World Fair, in 1900. The Fair exhibited some of the most technologically advanced inventions of the time — including diesel engines, talking films and escalators — as well as promoting a new artistic style: art nouveau.
The Musée d’Orsay was originally named the Gare d’Orsay and was one of the city’s main train stations. It opened in 1900, just in time for the Fair, and became a museum in 1986.

items.q: What was La Belle Époque?
o: A period of peace, prosperity and creativity from 1878 to 1914

items.q: What was the Eiffel Tower originally for?
o: A temporary entrance to the 1889 World Fair

items.q: What was the Musée d’Orsay before it was a museum?
What did the 1900 Fair exhibit?
o: Diesel engines, talking films and escalators

acts.title: La Belle Époque
tts: The French government had the Eiffel Tower built to celebrate the hundredth anniversary of the French revolution. At three hundred and twenty-four metres it was the tallest structure in the world for over forty years, and it was designed by Gustave Eiffel.
The Gare d’Orsay opened in 1900 and became a museum in 1986.
The first Métro line opened on the nineteenth of July 1900. Today the Paris metro has two hundred and fourteen kilometres of line and is used by almost one point four billion travellers every year.
The Belle Époque era ended in 1914, but it left an enduring legacy.

items.s: It was the tallest structure in the world for over ___ years.
The station became a museum in ___.
The first Métro line opened on ___ 1900.
The metro now carries almost ___ travellers a year.

acts.title: Concede, then turn
rule: Nobody changes their mind because they were contradicted. The move that works in English is a two-part one: give the other person something first, then take the argument somewhere else. Almost every phrase in this lesson is the first half of that pair.
points: You’ve got a point, but… Yes, but on the other hand… These are single moves, not two.
Accept the value, reject the sufficiency
I’m all for X, but I do want more than that. This is the most useful frame of all.
Don’t you think…? and isn’t it? invite agreement rather than demanding it.
No, but look… sounds blunt and is not: the look asks for attention, not obedience.
As I see it… It seems to me that… Both mark an opinion as an opinion.
eg: You’ve got a point, but they need more than that.
Concede, then turn.
Yes, but on the other hand, fun lessons can teach you nothing.
Concede, then turn.
I’m all for having fun, but I want more than that from a class.
Accept the value, reject the sufficiency.
Don’t you think you should change jobs if you hate it?
Invites agreement.
It is possible for a teacher to be too nice, isn’t it?
Question tag doing the same job.
No, but look — that isn’t quite the point.
Firm, but not aggressive.
As I see it, you need enough money, not a lot.
Marks an opinion as an opinion.
It seems to me that you have to enjoy it.
The same, slightly more formal.
Obviously that’s important.
Conceding fully, before returning to your own point.
I take your point about the salary.
A formal concession, useful in writing.
acts.careful: “You have a point but” with no pause and no development is not a concession — it is a formula. The concession only works if the next clause deals with something the first one actually raised.

items.q: You want to concede and then argue on.
o: You’ve got a point, but they need more than that.
You are wrong, but they need more.
That is a point of you, but…

items.q: You accept the value of something but not that it is enough.
o: I’m all for having fun, but I want more than that.
I am all for fun, but I want more of that.
I am all fun, but I want more.

items.q: You want to invite agreement rather than demand it.
o: Don’t you think you should change jobs?
You should change jobs, don’t you?

items.q: You are marking your view as a view.
o: As I see it, you need enough, not a lot.
How I see it, you need enough.
As I am seeing it, you need enough.

items.q: You disagree firmly but do not want to sound aggressive.
o: No, but look — that isn’t quite the point.
No. That is not the point.
You are not right about the point.

items.q: You are conceding formally, in writing.
o: I take your point about the salary.
I take your point of the salary.
I am taking your point about salary.

rows: Yes, but on the other hand…

lines: You’ve got a [point|reason|sense], but they need more than kindness.
Yes, but [on the other hand|in the other hand|on other hand], fun lessons can teach you nothing.
I’m all [for having|for have|to having] fun, but I want more than that.
The tower [was built|built|was build] as a temporary entrance, and the government [had it built|had built it|had it build] for the anniversary.

write.q: Write a summary of about 180 words of an argument you have read or heard recently — an article, a talk, a discussion at work. Report what the other side actually argues, concede what is genuinely right in it, and then give your own position. A summary reports before it judges: do not begin with your own view.
plan: what the other side argues, fairly stated
write.model:
The argument, made regularly at our management meetings, is that the company should stop paying for external training and put the money into salaries instead. The case rests on two points: that almost nobody applies what they learn, and that the people most likely to take a course are the people most likely to leave.

It is true that the second point is supported by our own figures. Of the eleven people who took an external qualification in the last four years, six have gone, and two of those went within a month of finishing.

However, the conclusion does not follow. Those six did not leave because they were trained; they left because nothing changed when they came back. A qualification with no new work attached to it is a leaving certificate, and that is a management failure rather than a training one.

As I see it, the budget should stay and the follow-up should be compulsory. Cutting the training would remove the symptom and leave the cause exactly where it is.

I am all for fun, but more of that.

o: Don’t you think you should change jobs?
You should change jobs, don’t you?

items.q: You are marking your view as a view.
You disagree firmly but not aggressively.
o: No. That is not the point.

items.q: You are conceding formally, in writing.
o: I take your point about the salary.
I take your point of the salary.
